options: Rate, I:E, PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), and Pmax
questions.explanation: Volume control targets tidal volume, while respiratory rate and inspiratory timing determine its delivery pattern. PEEP and a pressure limit or high-pressure alarm are also important settings, with the exact controls depending on the ventilator.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166

questions.stem: In VCV (volume-controlled ventilation), the Pmax limit is set at 35. A sudden kink occurs. What happens?
options: PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) rises to compensate
Volume stays fixed at any pressure
The vent switches to pressure support
Pressure hits the limit; volume falls
questions.explanation: A pressure limit prevents the ventilator from maintaining the set volume at unlimited pressure. If an obstruction causes the limit to be reached, delivery may be curtailed and tidal volume can fall; the exact response depends on the device.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Why is volutrauma the listed risk with PCV (pressure-controlled ventilation)?
options: Vt (tidal volume) rises if compliance suddenly improves
PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) is removed automatically
Flow is fixed so volume never varies
questions.explanation: Pressure control does not fix tidal volume. If compliance suddenly improves at the same pressure target, a larger volume may enter the lungs, creating an overdistension risk.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166

questions.stem: In PCV (pressure-controlled ventilation), the lecture's EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) target is about:
questions.explanation: An end-tidal CO2 around 35–40 mmHg is a common normal reference for an adult with adequate ventilation and perfusion. End-tidal CO2 does not always equal arterial CO2, especially with ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 10, printed pp. 243–244 (PaCO₂–PETCO₂ relationship and normal model)

questions.stem: On PCV-VG (pressure-controlled ventilation with volume guarantee), compliance worsens during insufflation. What does the ventilator do over the next few breaths?
options: Raise pressure to restore set Vt (tidal volume)
questions.explanation: PCV-VG adjusts inspiratory pressure over subsequent breaths to recover the selected tidal volume as compliance changes. When compliance worsens, pressure may increase within the ventilator’s limits.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Why is PCV (pressure-controlled ventilation) preferred for patients with an uncuffed ETT (endotracheal tube)?
options: VCV (volume-controlled ventilation) can’t be used with an ETT
questions.explanation: The slide lists uncuffed ETT/LMA (laryngeal mask airway) under high-pressure risks favoring PCV.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 6

questions.stem: A pregnant patient's large abdomen lowers compliance. Which mode is favored?
options: Volume control with high Vt (tidal volume)
questions.explanation: Pressure control can be useful in low-compliance conditions, including pregnancy in the cited discussion. Delivered volume still needs monitoring because maintaining pressure does not guarantee adequate ventilation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: On assist-control, an anxious patient breathes at 30/min. What is the risk?
questions.explanation: Assist-control can deliver a supported machine breath for each qualifying effort, so rapid triggering can cause excessive ventilation. If expiration becomes inadequate, closely spaced breaths can also produce air trapping or stacking.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 168–169

questions.stem: In ACV (assist-control ventilation), what happens if spontaneous effort is not detected?
options: Backup controlled breaths at the set RR (respiratory rate)
CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) is applied instead
questions.explanation: Assist-control retains a set mandatory rate. If patient effort is absent or not detected, controlled breaths are delivered at that backup rate.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: On an ACV (assist-control ventilation) pressure trace, what indicates a patient-triggered breath?
options: A small negative dip before the breath
A higher peak pressure than other breaths
questions.explanation: A small negative airway-pressure deflection before machine inflation indicates an inspiratory effort. In the illustrated pressure-triggered assist-control pattern, it distinguishes a patient-triggered breath.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: In SIMV (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation), spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths are delivered how?
options: At the full set tidal volume each time
At their own volume, with optional PS (pressure support)
At double the set tidal volume
questions.explanation: Spontaneous breaths between SIMV mandatory breaths are generated by the patient rather than automatically receiving the full mandatory tidal volume. Optional pressure support can augment those spontaneous breaths.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 169; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: A patient being weaned on SIMV (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation) with PS has rising RR (respiratory rate) and small spontaneous Vt (tidal volume). What is a reasonable step?
options: Switch to CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) of zero
questions.explanation: Rapid, small spontaneous breaths may indicate inadequate assistance or increased respiratory load. Reassess the cause and adequacy of ventilation; adjusting pressure support or mandatory support can be appropriate rather than removing assistance.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Which setting is part of PSV (pressure support ventilation) per the slide?
questions.explanation: Preset inspiratory time, peak pressure, trigger, backup RR (respiratory rate).
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 6

questions.stem: On standard PSV (pressure support ventilation) with an LMA (laryngeal mask airway), minute ventilation falls steadily. What should the provider do?
options: Increase FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) only and continue watching
Assist or switch to a mode with backup
questions.explanation: Falling minute ventilation on pressure support requires assessment and restoration of adequate ventilation. Assistance or a mode with suitable backup may be needed because PSV alone does not guarantee minute ventilation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: Pressure support helps patients overcome what?
options: Hypoxemia, by raising PaO2 (arterial partial pressure of oxygen) directly
questions.explanation: Pressure support adds inspiratory pressure to reduce the patient’s effort against airway and equipment resistance. It assists ventilation rather than directly measuring or guaranteeing arterial oxygen tension.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: In spontaneous mode, the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) is fully closed during a long case. What is the danger?
options: Loss of PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) from the open circuit
questions.explanation: In spontaneous or manual mode, the APL controls the circuit’s pressure-relief pathway. Excessive closure with continuing gas inflow can cause pressure accumulation and increase barotrauma risk.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 170; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 276

questions.stem: In spontaneous mode, what should be monitored closely?
options: Airway pressure, Vt (tidal volume), and RR (respiratory rate)
questions.explanation: Spontaneous breathing still requires monitoring of airway pressure, tidal volume, and respiratory rate. A fresh-gas setting alone cannot establish adequate patient ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 170

questions.stem: BiPAP (bilevel positive airway pressure) is useful when:
options: CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) fails or weaning support is needed
questions.explanation: BiPAP helps when CPAP fails or for continued weaning support.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 6

questions.stem: In CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), pressure greater than inspiratory airway pressure causes what?
questions.explanation: Gas flows into the patient when inspiratory airway pressure falls below the pressure available in the circuit. During CPAP, patient effort creates that relative pressure gradient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 170

questions.stem: APRV (airway pressure release ventilation) removes CO2 how?
questions.explanation: APRV maintains a higher pressure for recruitment and briefly releases to a lower pressure. Gas exits during the release, allowing CO2 elimination, with spontaneous breathing possible between releases.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 170–171

questions.stem: High-frequency ventilation uses which tidal volumes?
questions.explanation: High-frequency techniques use small tidal volumes at rapid rates. In oscillatory ventilation, delivered volumes can be smaller than anatomic dead space and gas transport uses additional mechanisms beyond ordinary bulk flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 170

questions.stem: HFV (high-frequency ventilation) is used when conventional ventilation fails, for certain procedures, or to:
questions.explanation: High-frequency techniques aim to provide gas exchange with small volumes and may reduce pressure-related injury in selected settings. The text also describes procedural uses and cautions that general clinical benefit in respiratory failure is not established.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160, 170

questions.stem: Anatomic recruitment with higher PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) may have which downside?
questions.explanation: Higher PEEP may open alveoli but also overdistend already open units and reduce venous return. Recruitment therefore needs to be balanced against adverse perfusion and hemodynamic effects.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: What does functional recruitment improve?
options: CO2 clearance from better ventilation and perfusion
Higher PaCO2 (arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide) from more dead space
questions.explanation: Functional recruitment improves volume and perfusion (CO2 clearance).
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 6

questions.stem: During a recruitment maneuver, BP (blood pressure) drops from 120/70 to 80/45. What is the mechanism?
options: Reduced preload from high intrathoracic pressure
questions.explanation: Increased intrathoracic pressure during recruitment can reduce venous return and preload. This can cause a substantial blood-pressure fall, particularly in a preload-sensitive patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: Which patient should NOT receive a recruitment maneuver?
options: Laparoscopic patient with falling SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation)
questions.explanation: Excessive inflation pressure and overdistension can disrupt alveolar structures and cause barotrauma, including pneumothorax. Pressure should be individualized because recruitment beyond the optimal point may instead overdistend already open alveoli.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, printed pp. 159–160

questions.stem: Recruitment maneuvers can be uncomfortable in which patients?
questions.explanation: Discomfort if awake or mildly sedated.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 6

questions.stem: For a 3-year-old on pressure control, which PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) limit fits the pediatric table?
questions.explanation: Pediatric PIP <28.
questions.citation: Course lecture, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 65

questions.stem: The pediatric table's initial FiO2 recommendation is:
options: 21% from the start to avoid toxicity
questions.explanation: FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen) 100% (quickly trend down).
questions.citation: Course lecture, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 65

questions.stem: Per the pediatric table, respiratory rate should be set to:
options: Normal rate for age or pathology
questions.explanation: RR parallels normal for age or pathophysiology.
questions.citation: Course lecture, Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 65

questions.stem: Which are execution or attention errors rather than knowledge errors? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Slips, capture errors, and faulty activation involve executing or initiating an action incorrectly despite an intended task. They differ from mistakes due to inadequate knowledge or a faulty mental model.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Which are human-factor causes of error? Select 2.
questions.explanation: The cited classification lists stress and ill health as human factors. It separately places noise and workplace constraints under environmental factors, and equipment design and false alarms under system factors.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Which reduce alarm fatigue? Select 3.
options: Lowering pulse ox volume to zero
questions.explanation: Alarm-fatigue reduction includes better prioritization and centralization, secondary notifications, and fewer false-positive alerts. Silencing alarms or indiscriminately widening every limit can hide meaningful deterioration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 389–390

questions.stem: Which should shape an SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) low alarm limit? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Alarm limits should consider the patient’s condition, how quickly saturation may change, and measurement-system delay. Alarm and clinician response time also matter because the warning must leave time for corrective action.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) is falling quickly along this curve. Which numbered alarm limit gives the most time to respond?
questions.explanation: Limit 1 is crossed first as the plotted saturation falls, providing the earliest warning and most potential response time. An appropriate limit must still balance early detection with the patient’s condition and false-alarm burden.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: A provider sets the limit at line 3 to avoid nuisance alarms. Given this curve, what is the problem?
options: Little time is left to correct the problem
The alarm will sound too often to be useful
The limit catches the event earliest
questions.explanation: Limit 3 is crossed last on the supplied falling-saturation curve, leaving the least time to respond. Lowering a threshold solely to avoid nuisance alarms can delay recognition of dangerous deterioration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: Which factor makes the steepness of this curve important when choosing a limit?
options: The number of alarms in the room
How fast the variable is changing
The cost of the monitoring system
questions.explanation: A steeper downward slope means saturation is decreasing more rapidly, shortening the interval between warning and critical hypoxemia. Alarm settings should account for the rate of change and patient condition.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: A sidestream analyzer adds a 15-second delay to this trend. How should limit 2 be adjusted?
options: Leave it alone, since delay doesn’t matter
Turn the alarm off and watch the trend instead
Move it farther from normal to cut false alarms
Move it closer to normal so it alarms earlier
questions.explanation: Moving the low-saturation alarm limit closer to the normal value provides earlier warning during a rapid decline. Alarm settings should account for the patient's condition, rate of change, measurement delay, and clinician response time while avoiding excessive nuisance alarms.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: A provider sets the vaporizer to 8% intending desflurane, but the sevo vaporizer is the one turned on. Which error type is this?
questions.explanation: A slip occurs when the intended task is appropriate but its execution is wrong. Activating sevoflurane when desflurane was intended is an execution error rather than a knowledge-based mistake.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider gives a drug believing it's safe in a patient with a contraindication they never learned about. Which error type?
questions.explanation: A mistake results from an inappropriate plan or judgment, often due to missing knowledge. Administering a contraindicated drug because the provider does not know the contraindication fits this category.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: During a crisis, a team keeps troubleshooting the pulse oximeter while the patient is in bronchospasm. Which error type?
questions.explanation: Fixation is persistent attention to an incorrect or less important explanation despite changing evidence. Troubleshooting the pulse oximeter while missing true bronchospasm delays treatment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider only looks at data that support "the patient is too light" and dismisses the falling EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide). Which error?
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias favors evidence supporting an existing hypothesis while discounting conflicting data. Ignoring falling end-tidal CO2 because it contradicts the presumed diagnosis illustrates this bias.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: The ventilator is left in manual mode after a break, but the provider assumes it's ventilating. Which error?
questions.explanation: A mode error occurs when an operator misidentifies the system's current state. Assuming automatic ventilation is active while the machine remains in manual mode risks failure to ventilate.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: "Give the antibiotic" is said when two antibiotics are drawn up. Which error type risks occurring?
questions.explanation: A description error is an ambiguous or incomplete specification of an intended action. Saying only 'the antibiotic' when two agents are prepared can cause the wrong medication to be selected.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider who always gives a relaxant right after induction does so on a case planned to keep the patient breathing spontaneously. Which error type is this?
questions.explanation: A capture error occurs when a familiar routine replaces the intended alternative. The habitual airway sequence can take over despite a deliberately changed plan.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider believes the APL (adjustable pressure-limiting valve) controls pressure during mechanical ventilation and keeps adjusting it to fix high pressures. Which error?
questions.explanation: A representational error is a faulty mental model of how equipment works. On many workstations the adjustable pressure-limiting valve controls manual ventilation, not the pressure of mechanically delivered breaths.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: After intubation, the provider forgets to turn on the ventilator. Which error type?
questions.explanation: Faulty activation includes failing to initiate an appropriate action. Forgetting to start mechanical ventilation after intubation is an omission of the required activation step.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Which error type is described as "cognitive lockup"?
questions.explanation: Fixation error is described as cognitive lockup: the clinician persists with an interpretation despite new evidence. Reassessment and attention to the most urgent problem are needed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider under the influence of a prescribed sedative makes an error. Which cause category applies?
questions.explanation: The textbook's human-error table categorizes impairment from prescribed or recreational substances under ill health. A sedating prescription can impair judgment and attention even when taken legally.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Moving the bed for a C-arm disconnects the circuit. Which cause of error is this?
questions.explanation: The textbook identifies circuit disconnection from moving equipment or personnel as a workplace-constraint error. Moving the bed for a C-arm can pull the breathing circuit apart.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Which is an environmental cause of error?
questions.explanation: Noise and miscommunication are environmental contributors to error. They can obscure verbal instructions and lead to a medication or treatment request being misunderstood.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Which is an equipment and system cause of error?
questions.explanation: False or excessively noisy alarms are equipment-and-system contributors to error. They can interfere with recognition of a true emergency and promote alarm fatigue.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Which practice directly addresses the lecture's equipment-design example?
questions.explanation: Note: check blade lights.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 17

questions.stem: Which practice best addresses the noise/miscommunication example?
options: Working faster to finish the task
Turning alarm volumes down in the room
Charting vital signs by hand more often
questions.explanation: Read-back prevents the misheard-antibiotic error.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 17

questions.stem: Recognizing a slow EtCO2 (end-tidal carbon dioxide) rise and predicting MH (malignant hyperthermia) before temperature climbs best reflects:
questions.explanation: Situation awareness combines understanding the present state with prior trends and likely future developments. Anticipating malignant hyperthermia from a rising end-tidal CO2 trend is forward-looking assessment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: A conscious effort to remain alert and select information defines:
questions.explanation: Attention is the conscious effort to remain alert and select relevant information. Vigilance extends this into sustained readiness to detect and respond to changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Forming the opinion "this hypotension is from hypovolemia" from the data defines:
questions.explanation: Judgment means forming an interpretation or evaluation from available evidence. Attributing hypotension to hypovolemia is a judgment; choosing a treatment is a separate decision.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Choosing to give a fluid bolus rather than a vasopressor based on your assessment is:
questions.explanation: Decision-making involves selecting among possible actions based on clinical judgment. Choosing a fluid bolus instead of a vasopressor is a treatment decision informed by the assessment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Interruptions and distractions fall into which factor category?
questions.explanation: Interruptions and distractions are task-and-information factors that affect vigilance. They divert attention from primary monitoring and can cause important changes to be missed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 374

questions.stem: Clumsy automation is which type of factor?
questions.explanation: Clumsy automation is a system-and-equipment factor affecting vigilance. Difficult interfaces or poorly designed automation can increase workload and promote errors.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 374

questions.stem: A night-shift provider after 20 hours awake is at higher risk mainly from which factors?
options: Fatigue, sleep loss, and circadian effects
questions.explanation: Fatigue, sleep loss, and circadian disruption are individual factors that impair sustained attention. Extended wakefulness during night work can slow detection and response.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 374–376

questions.stem: A faulty mental model of how the ventilator works is listed under which category?
questions.explanation: An incorrect understanding of ventilator operation is a faulty equipment mental model. The textbook lists such models among system-and-equipment factors affecting vigilance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 374

questions.stem: Which is an environmental factor affecting vigilance?
questions.explanation: Ambient temperature and humidity are environmental factors that influence vigilance. Uncomfortable operating-room conditions may distract or fatigue providers.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 374–375

questions.stem: Which is a human factor affecting vigilance?
questions.explanation: Boredom is an individual factor associated with reduced vigilance during prolonged low-workload monitoring. A stable case still requires attention because unexpected events can develop.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 374, 379

questions.stem: A provider turns the pulse oximeter tone off because it is "annoying." Which alarm function is lost?
options: Improving the accuracy of SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation)
Documenting events in the anesthetic record
Backing up a distracted or fatigued provider
questions.explanation: Audible pulse-oximeter information helps clinicians recognize oxygenation changes when attention is elsewhere. Turning the tone off removes a safeguard for a distracted or fatigued provider.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 386, 388

questions.stem: Two alarms sound identically during a crisis. Which design feature would help most?
questions.explanation: Distinctive acoustic patterns, pitches, and rhythms help identify the source and urgency of an alarm. Identical sounds can delay recognition during a crisis.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 387–388

questions.stem: While doing a complex regional block under ultrasound, a provider misses the BP (blood pressure) alarm. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Inattentional deafness is reduced recognition of an auditory signal during high visual workload. Concentrating on ultrasound guidance can therefore delay detection of a blood-pressure alarm.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 387

questions.stem: What can mask alarm tones in the OR (operating room)?
questions.explanation: High operating-room noise can mask or obscure auditory alarm tones. Appropriate sound design and audibility are needed so important warnings are not missed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 375, 387

questions.stem: Why is a patient with severe coronary disease given a tighter low-BP alarm limit?
options: Wider limits cause more false alarms
The patient's condition makes small drops dangerous
The monitor is less accurate in cardiac patients
questions.explanation: Alarm limits should reflect the patient's vulnerability to changes in the monitored variable. Severe coronary disease may make even modest hypotension important, supporting an individualized limit.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: Which limit-setting factor is about how long the provider takes to fix the problem?
options: Response time of the alarm system
Response time of the measurement system
Rate of change of the variable
questions.explanation: Alarm thresholds must account for the clinician's response and correction time. The warning should sound early enough to allow recognition and intervention.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: Which technique reduces bedside noise while keeping alarms detectable?
options: Turning all bedside alarms off at the start
Centralizing alarms and using visual alarms
questions.explanation: Centralized alarm management and visual indications can reduce bedside noise while preserving warnings. Important alarms must remain reliably detectable.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: Which strategy addresses alarm fatigue at its source?
options: Adding more alarms to every device
Silencing alarms whenever the patient is stable
Fewer false positives through design and maintenance
questions.explanation: Reducing false-positive alerts through design, maintenance, and individualized settings addresses a major source of alarm fatigue. Muting alarms or widening every limit can hide true deterioration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 389–390

questions.stem: Pagers and phones for alarms are an example of which strategy?
questions.explanation: Pagers and mobile phones are secondary notification systems. They route important alarms to responsible personnel without relying exclusively on loud bedside tones.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: How does adding sound-absorbing material help alarm design?
options: It replaces the need for visual alarms
It makes every alarm louder in the room
Less background noise lets alarms be quieter
It eliminates false alarms at the source
questions.explanation: Sound-absorbing materials reduce ambient noise, allowing alarms to remain audible at lower volumes. This improves the signal-to-noise ratio but does not prevent false alerts.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: After repeated false SpO2 (peripheral oxygen saturation) alarms, the provider widens the limit to 80%. Which risk results?
options: More false alarms during the case
questions.explanation: Repeated false alarms can encourage dangerously permissive limits. A low saturation threshold of 80% may delay recognition of real hypoxemia and leave little time to intervene.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 389–390

questions.stem: Which factor reflects workload from charting while managing an unstable patient?
questions.explanation: Secondary task intrusion occurs when another duty competes with the primary clinical task. Charting during instability can divert attention from monitoring and treatment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 374

questions.stem: "Training and experience" is listed among which factors?
questions.explanation: Training and experience are individual factors influencing vigilance and performance. They affect how efficiently providers recognize changes and respond to unfamiliar situations.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 374, 382

questions.stem: A drug swap in a crisis followed by refusing to reconsider the diagnosis shows which pairing?
options: Noise as a cause and slip as the error
Task complexity as a cause and mode error
Stress as a cause and fixation as the error
Ill health as a cause and mistake as the error
questions.explanation: Stress can contribute to drug or syringe swaps, as illustrated in the textbook's human-error table. Refusing to reconsider a diagnosis despite new evidence is fixation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 372–373

questions.stem: Monitoring differs from vigilance in that monitoring is:
options: The act of choosing between possible actions
A task of watching data streams for set changes
An awareness of where events are heading
A state of sustained readiness to respond
questions.explanation: Monitoring is the vigilance task of observing data streams to detect specified changes. Vigilance is broader: sustained readiness to recognize and respond.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Which situation does the third alarm function address?
questions.explanation: The third function of alarms is to assist when stress, workload, or limited training impairs detection or response. Alarms supplement clinical vigilance rather than replacing assessment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 386

questions.stem: Why are alarms most useful when they activate before a condition becomes critical?
options: Anticipating a crisis beats reacting to it
Early alarms reduce the cost of monitoring
Critical conditions can’t be treated anyway
Late alarms are more accurate than early ones
questions.explanation: Early alarms allow clinicians to recognize and correct deterioration before it becomes critical. Thresholds must balance timely warning against false alarms.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: Why might an experienced provider still miss an alarm during a difficult intubation?
options: Intubation lowers the volume of the monitors
Alarms are routinely silenced during intubation
High visual workload causes inattentional deafness
Experience reduces sensitivity to alarm tones
questions.explanation: High visual workload can produce inattentional deafness even in experienced providers. Difficult intubation can therefore delay recognition of an audible alarm.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 387

questions.stem: A provider fails to notice a slow BP (blood pressure) drop because attention is on the anesthesia record. Which cause applies?
options: Workplace constraints in the OR (operating room)
questions.explanation: The textbook classifies missing a change while manually recording vital signs as a human–machine function mismatch. Documentation can compete with direct monitoring.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: A provider dismisses a high-pressure alarm because "the surgeon is leaning on the chest" without checking the tube. If the tube was kinked, which error occurred?
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias occurs when a clinician accepts an explanation without seeking contradictory evidence. Assuming external chest pressure caused an alarm without checking for a kinked tube can delay correction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Which strategy most directly counters vigilance loss from boredom during a long stable case?
questions.explanation: Note: maintain vigilance, never get complacent.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment, 3rd ed., Ch. 17
